opus-5.5.text:
I think the core issue is that text and visual signals carry very different amounts of information, and they carry it in very different ways.

Text is a wonderful interface for humans. It's compact, it's abstract, and it lets you express intent at a high level, like "a dog running on the beach at sunset." But that sentence is massively underspecified. What kind of dog? Where is it in the frame? What is the camera angle, the lighting, the exact pose of the legs at each moment? A single sentence maps to an enormous space of possible images, and an even larger space of possible videos. So when you control generation with text, you're really giving the model a loose constraint and asking it to fill in almost everything else from its learned priors. That works well when you just want something plausible and beautiful, but it becomes very hard when you want something precise.

Visual signals are the opposite. If I give you a segmentation map, an edge map, a depth map, a pose skeleton, or a reference frame, I'm giving you dense, spatially aligned information. The model doesn't have to guess where things go. The correspondence between the condition and the output is pixel to pixel, or at least region to region. That's why, going back to our early work on things like pix2pixHD and GauGAN, you could get very controllable results. The user draws a layout, says "sky here, tree here, water here," and the model renders it. The control problem is much better posed.

So there's a tradeoff. Text is easy to provide but weak in precision. Visual signals are precise but costly for people to create. Most people can't draw a good depth map or animate a skeleton frame by frame.

With video the gap gets even bigger, because now you also have time. Describing motion in language is notoriously hard. "The person turns around slowly and then waves" leaves the timing, trajectory, and speed ambiguous. Physics, camera motion, and how objects interact are all very difficult to pin down with words alone. Visual conditions, like trajectories, camera paths, or a driving video, can specify those things directly.

There's also a data side. For text conditioning, you rely on captions, which are often noisy, incomplete, and describe only the salient parts of a scene. The model learns that text is only a partial description, so it learns to treat it loosely. For visual conditions, you can often derive them automatically from the data itself, running a depth estimator or pose estimator on real videos, so you get perfectly paired training data at scale. That makes the alignment much tighter.

My view is that the future isn't one or the other. Text is great for expressing intent and semantics; visual signals are great for geometry, layout, and motion. A good system should let you start with language, get something reasonable, and then refine with visual controls where precision matters. That's also very important for the physical AI work we care about. If you want to use world models to generate training data for robots or autonomous vehicles, you can't just say "a busy intersection." You need to control the exact layout, the agents, and their trajectories, so multimodal, especially visual, conditioning becomes essential.

r002.rationale: It says text and visual signals carry information in different ways and contrasts text’s underspecification with visual signals’ spatial detail as the source of control difficulty.

r003.rationale: It discusses noisy captions and tighter alignment from visual training data, but does not attribute greater data requirements for text conditioning to the structural mismatch between text and images or video.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I think about it is that text and visual signals sit at very different points on a spectrum of information density, and that gap is really the heart of the difficulty.

Text is extremely compressed. When I write "a woman walking a dog through a park at sunset," I've given the model maybe a dozen tokens, but the space of images consistent with that description is enormous. Where is she in the frame? What breed is the dog? How tall are the trees, where exactly is the sun, what's her posture mid-stride? Language leaves all of that unspecified. So the model has to fill in a huge amount, and it does so by sampling from what it has learned is plausible. That's wonderful when you want creativity, but it's a problem when you have a specific picture in your head. You end up in this loop of rewriting prompts, trying to coax out one particular detail, and language just isn't precise enough to pin it down. There's a reason designers draw sketches rather than describe them in paragraphs.

Visual signals are the opposite. A depth map, an edge map, a sketch, a pose skeleton, a reference frame, these carry spatial structure directly. They tell the model where things are and how they're arranged, which text is fundamentally bad at. Controlling with visual signals is much more about alignment: can the model respect the constraint you gave it while still generating something that looks real and coherent? That's a more tractable problem, in many ways, because the ambiguity is reduced.

Video makes all of this harder for a couple of reasons. One is time. Text describes an event, but it rarely describes how the event unfolds frame by frame. "A car turns left" doesn't tell you when the turn starts, how fast, or how the camera moves. So the temporal degrees of freedom explode, and language becomes an even weaker control signal than it is for images. The other is physics. In a single image you can get away with a lot, but in video the model has to maintain object permanence, consistent lighting, plausible motion, and errors compound across frames. Visual conditioning helps a lot there, because you can anchor the first frame, or give trajectories, or provide camera parameters, and suddenly the model has structure to hold onto.

So in practice I think the right answer isn't text versus visual signals, it's a combination. Text sets the semantics and the intent, the high-level "what." Visual signals provide the geometry, layout, and dynamics, the "where" and "how." The hard research question is how to make these controls compose cleanly, so a user can specify exactly as much as they want and let the model handle the rest. We're not fully there yet, especially for video, but that's the direction that makes these systems genuinely useful rather than just impressive.

astra-6.text:
I think the fundamental difficulty is that language and images describe things at different levels of precision. Text is very good at expressing a concept: you can say, “A person is walking down the street.” But that leaves many things unspecified. Where is the person in the frame? What is their pose? What does the street look like? The model has to fill in all those details.

And sometimes you have a very specific image in your mind, but describing it in words is surprisingly difficult. With a visual signal—a sketch, a reference image, or a pose—you can communicate the spatial structure much more directly. Instead of explaining where every object should go, you can show it.

For video, there’s an additional challenge because you need to control how things change over time. A sentence can describe an action, but it usually doesn’t specify the exact trajectory, timing, or camera movement. The model has to interpret those choices while keeping the scene consistent.

So I see text and visual signals as complementary. Text is a convenient way to communicate what you want, and visual inputs can help specify precisely how you want it to look or move.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the fundamental difficulty is that language and images describe the world at very different levels of detail. With text, you can say, “A person is walking down the street,” but that leaves many things unspecified: what the person looks like, where they are in the frame, what the street looks like, and how the camera moves. The model has to fill in those details. That flexibility is useful for creativity, but it makes precise control difficult.

Visual signals can communicate some of those constraints much more directly. A reference image can show appearance and composition; a sketch can show spatial structure. Describing the same information in words might take a long paragraph and still be ambiguous.

For video, you also have the temporal dimension. You need to control not only what appears, but how it moves and how its appearance stays consistent over time. Even a reference image doesn’t specify all of that.

So I see text and visual inputs as complementary. Text is a convenient way to express intent, while visual signals can provide concrete constraints. The challenge is getting the model to combine them so the user can control the details they care about while leaving room for the model to generate the rest.
